faq.contacts.p3: The system is designed so that you can't message a random person, even knowing their username. To start a conversation, one of you must share a QR code or an invite link, and the other must scan or follow it. Codes and links are temporary — they expire in 5 minutes. In the future they'll become single-use as well, so a leaked link can't trigger a spam attack.
faq.contacts.p5: It's an intentional design choice. In most messengers, knowing someone's phone number or username is enough to start flooding them with messages. Here, mutual consent is baked into the architecture — not just declared in a privacy policy.
faq.contacts.p7: The code only lives for 5 minutes — even if intercepted, the window is very short. Once someone adds you, you'll see a new conversation and can immediately block them. Single-use codes will completely close this scenario in the future.
faq.contacts.q4: Why this restriction? Isn't it inconvenient?
faq.contacts.q6: What if someone shares my QR code without my permission?
faq.demo-title.t2: An interactive cryptography demo shows how key exchange, Double Ratchet, and post-quantum algorithms work step by step. Available for testers and the curious.
faq.demo-title.want-to-see-it-in-action: Want to see it in action?
faq.encryption.p10: Honest limits: Stealth hides the sender identity from the server, not message timing, size, or your IP address — those remain visible at the network/transport layer. Privacy Pass tokens can ride along for anti-spam; server-side enforcement is still rolling out, so treat token-based rate control as maturing, not finished.
faq.encryption.p12: No — none. No analytics, no usage metrics, no behavioural events, no crash phone-home, no advertising identifiers. Not "collected and anonymised" — not collected. The app has no third-party trackers (no Firebase, Crashlytics, Sentry, Amplitude, Segment); its only external dependencies are transport/media infrastructure and an on-device ML library. Production builds also write no diagnostic logs to disk and expose no debug or log-export screen. When we need logs to fix a bug, it is you who taps "share" in a beta build — never a silent upload.
faq.encryption.p3: All messages are encrypted on the sender's device before transmission and can only be decrypted on the recipient's device. The server sees only an encrypted stream and routes it — it cannot read content technically, not just by policy. For key establishment, Konstruct uses X3DH extended with a post-quantum protocol (PQXDH) — protecting against "record now, decrypt with quantum computer later" attacks. Messages use Double Ratchet, which rotates keys with every message, so compromising one key doesn't expose past or future messages (forward secrecy + break-in recovery).
faq.encryption.p5: The server sees: that device A transmitted encrypted bytes to device B, the approximate size, and a timestamp. It doesn't see: message content, names, avatars, or Display Names. Messages aren't stored on the server after delivery. Usernames are stored only for routing purposes and aren't connected to real identities.
faq.encryption.p7: This is the harder part. The server can still observe that someone delivered ciphertext to device B (recipient, time, size). With always-on Stealth (sealed sender), it does not learn who sent that ciphertext — see the next question. VEIL partially obscures the network path. Full anonymity at the routing layer (hiding from the recipient's side and from network-level IP/timing correlation too) is a problem of a different order of magnitude and isn't solved today.
faq.encryption.p9: Yes — and it is always on for eligible traffic (user messages, receipts, call signaling, profile shares). There is no user toggle in production: the device leaves the sender field out of the envelope and seals a signed sender certificate to the recipient's identity key. The recipient decrypts and verifies who sent it; the server cannot. A few control paths (e.g. E2E heartbeats, multi-device sync, pure session control) stay identified by design.

faq.messages.p4: Yes, editing is supported. After changes, the message is marked as "edited". The edit propagates to the recipient's device through the same delivery mechanism as regular messages.
faq.messages.p6: Notifications are delivered through Apple Push Notification Service (APNs). A stable internet connection is required. If the phone is in airplane mode, behind a VPN with aggressive filtering, or Apple decided the push was "low priority" — the notification may be delayed or not arrive at all. When the app opens again, messages sync automatically.

faq.messages.status.list:
• Sending — message is being encrypted and sent to the server
  • Sent — server accepted the message
  • Delivered — the recipient's app received and decrypted it
  • Read — the recipient opened the chat and saw the message
faq.messages.status.note: "Delivered" and "Read" are acknowledgements (ACKs) sent back through the same encrypted channel.

faq.profile.p3: Display Name and avatar are stored only on your device — they never go to the server. When you start a new conversation, the other person sees only a generated pseudonym (deterministic — always the same for a given ID). If you want them to see your real name and photo, go to their profile and tap "Share Profile" — your Display Name and avatar will be sent directly over the encrypted channel.
faq.profile.p5: A blank name would be awkward — you'd see featureless rows in your chat list with no way to tell contacts apart. The generated name is stable: "Quick Falcon" is always "Quick Falcon" for that ID, on any device. That's more useful than a raw UUID.
faq.profile.p7: Yes. Display priority: Display Name (if they shared it) → username → generated name. So if someone registered with @john, you'll see that, not "Peaceful Whale".
faq.profile.q2: What is the Display Name for?

faq.registration.p3: During registration, the app receives a cryptographic Proof of Work challenge from the server and solves it — this prevents automated bot registrations. At the same time, several cryptographic key sets are generated on-device: long-term identity keys, signed prekeys, and one-time prekeys (including post-quantum ML-KEM-768 keys). Only the public parts of these keys and the PoW result are sent to the server. Private keys never leave your device. Your identity is these keys — there's no password to steal or recover.
faq.registration.p5: Not yet. In conventional messengers, "sign out and back in" means entering a username and password. Here your identity is the cryptographic keys stored on your device — without them, you can't authenticate. Deleting the app is equivalent to losing your account.
faq.registration.p7: In Settings you can generate a seed phrase — a sequence of words that can reconstruct your private keys. It works the same way as a recovery phrase in crypto wallets. Write it down and keep it somewhere safe — this is the only way to transfer your account to a new device.

faq.resilience.donate.p: No ads, no data resale, no telemetry — the flip side is that Konstruct runs on voluntary donations. They go directly to development and the server. Prefer Monero (XMR) if you care about privacy — unlike Bitcoin its chain isn't public. Always cross-check an address against the project repository before sending, in case a page is tampered with.
faq.resilience.p3: Today: alpha runs on a single trusted server — if it goes offline, messaging stops until it returns. The target architecture is three tiers of graceful degradation: federated servers (planned 2027 — anyone can run one, so even if the founding team's server goes down, community servers continue); VEIL relay nodes (planned — lightweight relay nodes that route messages without storing anything, designed to run on hardware as small as a Raspberry Pi); direct P2P (planned — when both users are online simultaneously, messages will travel directly between devices over QUIC/VEIL with no server involved). Once all three tiers ship, two users will be able to communicate as long as they have internet access, regardless of central infrastructure.
faq.resilience.p5: Yes — unconditionally. Sending messages, receiving messages, E2EE, and all security features will never go behind a paywall. Donation-only models have historically proved fragile for privacy projects, so Konstruct plans a mix: voluntary donations, optional premium features (larger file transfers, extended history, custom themes — never security features), and B2B hosted instances for organizations. The core will always be free.
faq.resilience.p8: P2P mode is planned, not yet implemented — all traffic currently goes through the central server. The target design: when both users are simultaneously online and connected to a Konstruct server, the server will signal them to upgrade to a direct peer-to-peer QUIC/VEIL connection. Once established, the server exits the message relay path — traffic flows directly between devices. If either user goes offline, the server automatically resumes relaying. The encryption (Signal Protocol) is identical in both modes — the server was never able to read message content either way. P2P is planned for desktop clients first (always-on connection); mobile clients will support short P2P bursts when both have the app open.

faq.security.p3: For this, the app has Lockdown Mode. When enabled, notifications only come from people who were in your contacts at activation time. Messages from new senders are still saved — they just won't disturb you. Useful if you're a public figure and want to temporarily close off from new contacts.
faq.security.p5: If a suspiciously high number of messages arrives from a single sender in a short time (more than ~10 in 30 seconds), the client automatically shows a warning and mutes notifications from them. You can then allow them (if it was a glitch) or block them. Importantly: this is receiver-side protection and works regardless of what client the attacker uses.

faq.t2: How Konstruct works, why it works this way, and answers from users and testers.
faq.technical.p3: A session is an established encrypted channel between two devices. It's built on one-time keys that can't be reused, and keys rotate with every message. If the app was inactive for a long time, the device was reinstalled, or state desynchronization occurred — the session may stop decrypting incoming messages. In this case, automatic session healing kicks in: the app renegotiates keys and restores the channel in the background. Usually the user notices nothing — messages just start arriving again.
faq.technical.p5: Sync between multiple devices (phone + desktop) is in development. The desktop app exists as a prototype. Since identity is tied to keys rather than a server account, multi-device support requires a separate key-binding mechanism — we're working on it.
faq.technical.p7: Live messaging is a gRPC bidirectional MessageStream — one long-lived stream for heartbeats, inbound messages, and delivery receipts — not request/response polling. On current iOS builds the production path is QUIC (ConstructEngine); if QUIC is blocked or the handshake fails, the client falls back to gRPC over HTTP/2 + TLS 1.3 automatically. End-to-end encryption is independent of the transport: the wire only carries sealed ciphertext. That combination (modern gRPC bidi + QUIC) is uncommon among consumer privacy messengers, which typically use REST/JSON or proprietary TCP stacks.

The more precise the description (what you did, what you expected, what happened), the faster we can investigate. For a session issue, include logs from both devices.

faq.veil.p2: VEIL — Variable Encoded Interface Layer. In Konstruct, VEIL serves two roles: (1) a transport layer that disguises messenger traffic as ordinary background noise, defeating DPI systems and censorship firewalls; (2) a relay tier — when a direct connection to the main server is unavailable, VEIL relay nodes can route traffic. Even if packets are intercepted, they look like random data, not messenger traffic.
faq.veil.p4: It's configurable. Under normal conditions you can use a direct connection — it's faster. VEIL activates automatically or manually when a direct connection is unavailable or undesirable. Today VEIL's obfs4/WebTunnel transport is deployed but currently throttled by active DPI in some regions; a replacement — veil-front — is implemented and validated on real devices, with public rollout in progress.
faq.veil.q3: Is VEIL always on or only during blocks?
home.about.t10: Unlike centralized platforms, Konstruct is designed for federation — eventually you will be able to choose or run your own server (you@your-server.example). The server is blind to message content: it stores only public keys and encrypted ciphertext, never plaintext. Sender-side metadata minimisation uses always-on sealed sender (Stealth) for eligible traffic — the server does not see who sent a message, only the recipient, arrival time, and size (honest limits: timing/IP still visible on the wire). A future release will also support direct peer-to-peer delivery when both parties are online, removing the server from the data path entirely. Federation and P2P are part of the 2027 roadmap; today the network is a single trusted server.
home.about.t11: Three lines we will not cross. The state must not monopolize information exchange. Corporations must not build apps engineered for infinite scroll. Your data is yours — not someone else's digital oil. Konstruct is built around those constraints, not around engagement metrics.
home.about.t2: Privacy and security are not optional. In an era of mass surveillance, data breaches, and emerging quantum computing threats, communication privacy is more critical than ever.
home.about.t3: Konstruct is built on cryptographic principles we treat as invariant:
home.about.t4: 1. No safe backdoors. Any intentional weakening of encryption — regardless of pretext — creates a vulnerability that will be exploited by adversaries. E2EE must be absolute and verifiable.
home.about.t5: 2. Privacy-by-default. The system must protect confidentiality without requiring user action or justification. Privacy is a property of the protocol, not a setting.
home.about.t6: 3. Server-blind architecture. The server must be technically incapable of reading content, resolving group membership, or exposing decryptable metadata. Trusting the operator is not a substitute for cryptographic guarantees.
home.about.t7: 4. Decentralisation by design. Centralised platforms present a single point of legal and technical pressure. Federated and P2P topologies distribute trust and eliminate censurability at the protocol level.
home.about.t8: 5. Post-quantum readiness. "Capture now, decrypt later" is an active threat model. Hybrid post-quantum key exchange must be integrated today to protect data against future cryptanalytic breakthroughs.
home.about.t9: Konstruct implements these principles using the Signal Protocol design (X3DH handshake + Double Ratchet) — the same end-to-end encryption design that powers Signal and WhatsApp — implemented from scratch in Rust. We extend it with a hybrid post-quantum KEM (ML-KEM-768, NIST FIPS 203) so that traffic recorded today remains protected once cryptographically relevant quantum computers exist.
home.comparison.t9:
* Telegram E2EE only in "Secret Chats", not default.
† Session also requires no phone number — that is its main pitch. Session V1 still uses static long-term keys with no forward secrecy or post-compromise security. Anonymity without forward secrecy is a compromise, not a full answer; Konstruct aims for both (Signal Protocol design + no required identifier).
‡ Konstruct's PQ KEM (ML-KEM-768) is opt-in and deployed; PQ signatures (ML-DSA-65) have working crypto and server-side verification — client rotation orchestration is still in progress.
Live messaging uses a gRPC bidirectional stream on QUIC (HTTP/2 fallback) — not REST/JSON polling.
home.features.t2: End-to-end encryption by default — servers see only encrypted blobs.
home.features.t3: Forward secrecy — past messages stay secure even if keys leak.
home.features.t4: Post-quantum key exchange — hybrid X25519 + ML-KEM-768 (Kyber-768). Signatures are Ed25519 today; ML-DSA-65 (Dilithium-3) for hybrid signatures is planned.
home.features.t5: Federation — run your own server or use a trusted provider, with email-like addressing.
home.features.t6: Lightweight server — Rust-based, minimal resource use, easy self-hosting.
home.features.t7: Zen UI — no notification spam, no social noise, focus on calm interaction.
home.features.t8: Modern live transport — gRPC bidirectional MessageStream over QUIC (HTTP/2 fallback), VEIL when the path is censored, direct P2P planned when both peers are online.
home.get-involved.t2: Konstruct is open source under weak-copyleft licenses: MPL-2.0 for the client apps and VEIL, AGPL-3.0 for the server and relay, Apache-2.0 for shared libraries, and CC-BY-4.0 for text / specs. Privacy technology should be transparent and auditable by anyone — including the open issues we haven't fixed yet.
home.get-involved.t3: Contributions welcome — from code improvements to security review to documentation. We are a tiny team; PRs and issues are read by humans, not triaged by a queue.
home.get-involved.t7: Report a security issue (GitHub private advisory)
home.how-it-works.t11: gRPC bidirectional MessageStream over QUIC — live production path on iOS (ConstructEngine / construct-transport). One long-lived stream carries heartbeats, inbound messages, and delivery receipts without opening a new TCP handshake per event. QUIC brings connection migration, multiplexed streams, and faster recovery on lossy or long-haul links (validated intercontinentally, e.g. Australia → EU edge).
home.how-it-works.t12: gRPC over HTTP/2 (TLS 1.3): automatic fallback when QUIC is blocked or handshakes time out — same protobuf contracts, same E2EE payload, no user toggle.
home.how-it-works.t13: Why this is a product edge: mainstream privacy messengers still lean on REST/JSON (Signal-class stacks) or closed proprietary wire formats (WhatsApp, Telegram MTProto). Shipping a modern gRPC bidi + QUIC live path is rare in consumer messaging — lower framing overhead, fewer reconnect storms, and a stack that matches how high-performance services are built today. E2EE stays on top; transport only moves sealed ciphertext.
home.how-it-works.t14: VEIL (anti-censorship): traffic obfuscation when direct TLS is throttled or blocked. Today: obfs4 + WebTunnel pluggable transports, currently throttled by active DPI in some regions. veil-front, an honest-front HTTPS layer that makes tunnelled traffic indistinguishable from a real public web service, is implemented and validated on real devices with provisioned tickets; public rollout is in progress.
home.how-it-works.t2: Konstruct uses gRPC with Protocol Buffers for efficient binary framing, and keeps a persistent bidirectional MessageStream open for real-time delivery — not request/response polling. The backend is split into independent microservices (auth, user, messaging, signaling, media) for fault isolation. Most consumer messengers still ship REST/JSON or proprietary TCP stacks; Konstruct’s live path is gRPC bidi over QUIC, with HTTP/2 as automatic fallback.
home.how-it-works.t4: X3DH + Double Ratchet (Signal Protocol design): end-to-end encryption with forward secrecy and post-compromise security (self-healing).
home.how-it-works.t5: Hybrid Post-Quantum KEM: X25519 classical + ML-KEM-768 (NIST FIPS 203, Kyber-768) for key exchange. If either component is broken, the other still protects.
home.how-it-works.t6: Authentication signatures: Ed25519 today. Hybrid ML-DSA-65 (Dilithium-3, NIST FIPS 204) signing and verification are implemented and cross-verified between client and server; client-side key rotation orchestration is still in progress.
home.how-it-works.t7: AEAD: ChaCha20-Poly1305 for message encryption. KDF: HKDF-SHA256 with domain-separation labels per protocol section. Anti-spam PoW: Argon2id.
home.how-it-works.t8: Server is blind to content: messages are stored only as ciphertext; the server cannot decrypt. By default the server still sees delivery timestamps and recipient for routing. Eligible user traffic uses always-on sealed sender (Stealth) so the envelope omits the sender id — only the recipient can unseal who wrote. Privacy Pass anti-spam tokens can accompany sealed sends; server-side token enforcement is still rolling out.
home.how-it-works.t9: Crypto Agility: versioned protocol suites allow algorithm upgrades without rebuilding client apps.
home.identity.address: Your address is a choice, not an assignment. Federated addressing (you@your-server.example) means the namespace you live in is one you picked or run yourself. No operator can revoke who you are, only where you happen to be reachable (federation is on the 2027 roadmap).
home.identity.authorship: Your authorship is separable from your message. Always-on sealed sender removes the sender identity from the stored envelope. The recipient can unseal who wrote; the server cannot. Being read and being identified are different events, and we treat them as such.
home.identity.continuity: Your continuity is distributed, not held. Social recovery (BIP39 / SLIP-39) reconstructs access from fragments you entrusted to people you chose — no company holds the master copy of you, because no master copy exists (in development).
home.identity.discovery: How people find each other. Without a phone book there is no cold outreach: conversations start with a temporary QR code or invite link (mutual consent; codes expire in minutes). An optional username is a convenience alias only — not required to exist. When federation ships, addresses will look like email and can be dictated over the phone (you@your-server.example).
home.identity.keypair: Your identity is a keypair. Nothing else is required. No phone number. No email. Not even a username — an identifier is something you may add for convenience, never something the system demands in order to exist. Signal, WhatsApp and Telegram all bind you to a phone number, which means a subpoena to a carrier is a subpoena to your identity. Here there is no carrier in the loop, because there is no number in the loop. Your account is cryptographic material you generated on your own device, and the server learns only the public half.
home.identity.lead: Every centralised platform starts from the same assumption: that "you" are a row in its database — a phone number, a profile, a graph of contacts it owns and can hand over. Konstruct rejects that premise at registration. There is no canonical record of you anywhere in this system, because there is nothing to record.
home.identity.limit: The honest limit: cryptography cannot make you unobservable. Timing and IP correlation remain visible on the wire, and a sufficiently resourced adversary works at that layer, not this one. What we can guarantee is narrower and worth stating plainly — no component of this system is designed to accumulate you.

home.meta.title: Konstruct - Privacy-First Secure Messenger with Post-Quantum Encryption
home.resilience.t2: Centralised privacy projects are fragile: when funding dries up or a single operator is compelled to shut down, the network goes with them. Konstruct is designed around the opposite principle — as components disappear, the rest keeps working. The target architecture is three tiers, each with the same end-to-end cryptographic guarantees regardless of delivery path. Today only Tier 1 with a single trusted server is live; Tiers 2 and 3 are on the roadmap.
home.resilience.t3: Tier 1 — Federated servers (planned 2027): anyone will be able to run a Konstruct server with an email-style address (you@your-server.example). If the founding team disappears, community-operated nodes can keep the network alive.
home.resilience.t4: Tier 2 — Community relay nodes (planned 2027): lightweight relays (designed to run on hardware as small as a Raspberry Pi) will provide message routing without a full server — no user database, no key storage.
home.resilience.t5: Tier 3 — Direct P2P (planned 2027+): when both users are online, messages will travel directly between devices over QUIC/ICE — the server steps out of the data path entirely.
home.resilience.t6: The Signal Protocol design (X3DH + Double Ratchet + hybrid PQ KEM) is transport-agnostic: whether messages travel through a server, a relay node, or directly between devices, the cryptographic guarantees stay the same.
home.roadmap.t10: Privacy Pass token enforcement (anti-spam on the always-on sealed-sender path) · desktop applications for Windows, Linux · formal verification (Kani).
home.roadmap.t11: Honest current status: alpha. iOS via TestFlight only (join the beta); no public App Store release yet. macOS Desktop client is in active development, no build available yet. Single trusted server (no federation). VEIL obfs4 transport is deployed but currently throttled by active DPI in some regions; the veil-front replacement is implemented and validated on-device, with public ticket rollout in progress. Not recommended for adversarial threat models until first external audit completes.
home.roadmap.t2: Done (H1 2026): gRPC/Protobuf · live gRPC bidi MessageStream over QUIC (HTTP/2 fallback; intercontinental production validation) · X3DH + Double Ratchet · hybrid PQXDH with ML-KEM-768 (opt-in) · session healing · WebRTC voice/video calls with E2EE signaling · iOS TestFlight beta · VEIL anti-censorship (obfs4, WebTunnel) · veil-front implemented and validated on-device · always-on Stealth (sealed sender) for eligible traffic.
home.roadmap.t3: In progress: veil-front public ticket rollout · macOS Desktop client (iOS-direct crypto path, no public build yet) · Android client (currently Phase 0 — Rust core builds, Kotlin wrapper TBD) · BIP39 / SLIP-39 social recovery · MLS group chats (RFC 9420) · first external security audit · hybrid PQ signatures (ML-DSA-65) — crypto core and server storage /verification implemented, client-side orchestration (identity generation, key rotation) not yet wired into the shared core.
home.roadmap.t5: Phase 1 — Core Relay (H2 2026): standalone construct-relay binary deployable on a \$5 VPS or Raspberry Pi · single Docker container, no Kafka/Redis/PostgreSQL required · preserves all E2EE guarantees · federation gateway for backward compatibility.
home.roadmap.t6: Phase 2 — DHT & Discovery (2027): Kademlia DHT overlay for peer discovery and responsible-node routing · signed user records in DHT · offline message storage with replication · bootstrap node network.
home.roadmap.t7: Phase 3 — Hybrid Routing & P2P (2027): direct peer-to-peer delivery via libp2p hole-punching · automatic fallback to relay routing · online presence in DHT · client multi-relay support.
home.roadmap.t8: Phase 4 — Ecosystem (2027–2028): public seed nodes · spam resistance (RLN / proof-of-work) · MLS group chats over decentralised transport · reputation for relay operators · external security audit.

Prefer Monero if you value privacy: unlike Bitcoin, its chain is not public, so your donation isn't linkable and the balance isn't visible.

home.t4: Identity is a construct — not a phone number in someone else's database. Konstruct is an open-source encrypted messenger built on the Signal Protocol design (X3DH + Double Ratchet) with hybrid post-quantum key exchange (ML-KEM-768). The state must not monopolize information exchange. Corporations must not build apps engineered for infinite scroll. Your data is yours — not digital oil.
home.telemetry.t2: Konstruct collects no analytics, no usage metrics, no behavioural events, no crash phone-home and no advertising identifiers. Not "collected and anonymised" — not collected. This is possible because we are not funded by advertising or data resale, so there is no reason to watch you, and the app is built so we can't.
home.telemetry.t3: No third-party SDKs. No Firebase, Crashlytics, Sentry, Amplitude, Segment — no tracker of any kind. The app's only external dependencies are transport and media infrastructure (gRPC, WebRTC) and an on-device ML library. No ATT prompt, no SKAdNetwork.
home.telemetry.t4: Production keeps no logs. Release builds write no diagnostic log to disk and expose no debug or log-export surface. When we need logs to fix a bug, it is you who taps "share" in a beta build — never a silent background upload.
home.telemetry.t5: Honest about what the server must see. To route ciphertext the server necessarily holds a small, fixed set of metadata (recipient, timing, size, your public keys, push token) — always-on sealed sender removes even who sent a message from the stored envelope. What we don't yet fully solve (timing/IP correlation) lives in our Privacy Policy, not in a marketing promise.
